about: CK-F, the Foundations checkpoint (curriculum v2 §3.3): nine short tasks on unfamiliar situations across T0-T6 and N1, then the main estimate (a town's school buses go electric). Prairie Town is fictional; its numbers are illustrative. The two charts use real Southwest Power Pool shapes (EIA-930, 2025) scaled to Prairie Town as in lesson 0 (450 MW = SPP's 2025 peak hour); _tests/learn/test_ck-f-estimate.js checks them against town_year.json and town_days.json and checks every answer below.

tasks.title: Why balance every moment?
tasks.prompt: In one or two sentences: why must supply equal demand at every moment on a power grid, and what tells the operator when it does not?
points: The grid stores almost no energy, so power has to be made at the moment it is used.
The frequency shows a gap: it falls below 60 Hz when demand runs ahead of supply, and rises above 60 Hz when supply runs ahead.
tasks.solution: The grid stores almost nothing, so every MW used must be made at that moment. A mismatch shows up in the frequency: below 60 Hz when demand runs ahead of supply, above 60 Hz when supply runs ahead.

tasks.title: Phone charges in a day
tasks.prompt: A U.S. home uses about 10,800 kWh of electricity a year. A phone takes about 15 Wh for a full charge (illustrative). About how many full charges equal one day of the home's use?

why.a: That forgets that 1 kWh is 1,000 Wh.
why.b: That is one hour of the home's use, not a day.
why.c: One day is about 30 kWh, or 30,000 Wh.
why.d: That is a whole year, not one day.

tasks.solution: One day: 10,800 kWh ÷ 365 ≈ 30 kWh = 30,000 Wh. Full charges: 30,000 Wh ÷ 15 Wh ≈ 2,000. The trap is the k: kWh and Wh differ by a factor of 1,000.

tasks.title: A December day's demand
tasks.prompt: The chart shows Prairie Town's demand on a real December weekday. When is demand highest, and how much above the day's lowest hour?
options: 07:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour
19:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour
14:00, about a quarter above the lowest hour

why.b: The axis starts at 260 MW, not zero, so the line exaggerates the swing.
why.c: 19:00 is the evening hump, lower than the morning peak.

tasks.solution: Peak: 347 MW at 07:00, when heating and the morning rush coincide. Low: 282 MW at 14:00 and 15:00. Ratio: 347 ÷ 282 ≈ 1.23, about a quarter higher. Always read where the axis starts: here at 260 MW.

tasks.title: After a plant trips
tasks.prompt: A 60 MW gas unit in Prairie Town's region trips. Put what happens next in order, first at the top.
items: The frequency starts to fall below 60 Hz.
Within seconds, governors on running plants raise their output and the fall stops.
Within minutes, the operator's control system orders reserve plants up to replace the lost 60 MW.
The frequency is back at 60 Hz, and the operator restores its reserves for the next trip.
tasks.solution: Fall first, then the automatic response of governors within seconds, which stops the fall but does not restore 60 Hz. The operator's reserves replace the lost power over minutes, and only then are the reserves rebuilt.

tasks.title: Forecast against actual
tasks.prompt: The chart shows the day-ahead forecast and the actual demand of a real spring day, scaled to Prairie Town. Over the day, the forecast was mostly…
options: too low, by at most about 2% of demand
too high, by at most about 2% of demand
too low, by up to about 20% of demand

why.a: Actual demand sits above the forecast in most hours, by at most 6 MW.
why.b: Look at which line is on top: actual demand is above the forecast.
why.c: The largest gap is 6 MW on about 290 MW: about 2%.
why.d: The two lines differ in most hours.

tasks.solution: Actual demand is above the forecast in 19 of 24 hours. The largest miss is 6 MW at 13:00 and 14:00, about 2% of demand. Operators hold reserves to cover misses like these.

tasks.title: A wind farm's year
tasks.prompt: A 50 MW wind farm runs at the 2025 U.S. average capacity factor for wind, 33.8%. About how much energy does it make in a year?
tasks.solution: 50 MW × 8,760 h × 0.338 ≈ 148,000 MWh, or 148 GWh. Without the capacity factor you would get 438,000 MWh: the farm at full output every hour, which no wind farm does.

tasks.title: A windless winter evening
tasks.prompt: A windless winter evening at 18:00, with demand near its peak. Which pair of plants can Prairie Town count on to be there?
options: The solar farm and the wind farm
The gas peaker and the nuclear plant
The wind farm and the nuclear plant
Rooftop solar and the gas peaker

why.a: The sun is down and the wind is calm.
why.b: Both can run whatever the weather, unless they are on outage: that is firm capacity.
why.c: The wind is calm, so the wind farm makes almost nothing.
why.d: The sun is down at 18:00 in winter.

tasks.solution: Firm capacity is output you can count on when it is needed, whatever the weather, unless the plant is on outage. At a calm winter dusk that means the gas peaker and the nuclear plant; wind and solar do other jobs.

tasks.title: Spot the error in a headline
tasks.prompt: Composite headline (not a real story): “New 100 MW solar farm will power 100,000 homes all year.” At the 2025 U.S. solar capacity factor of 24.0% and 10,800 kWh per home a year, about how many homes' yearly use does it make?

why.a: Too few: check the hours in a year, 8,760.
why.b: About 210,000 MWh a year, divided by 10.8 MWh per home.
why.c: That is the headline, which counts the farm at full output.
why.d: That is ten times too many: check MW against kW.

tasks.solution: 100 MW × 8,760 h × 0.240 ≈ 210,000 MWh a year; ÷ 10.8 MWh per home ≈ 19,500 homes. The headline treats the nameplate as output, the lens's physics question, and “all year” hides that solar makes nothing at night.

tasks.title: The school-bus estimate
tasks.prompt: Prairie Town's 20 diesel school buses are replaced by electric buses. Estimate the electricity the 20 buses will use in a year. Give a low and a high value with units, the main uncertainty, and one way to check. Make and state your own assumptions.
